title: Macrina the teacher
hookLine: Basil and Gregory of Nyssa's older sister taught them both
tomorrow: Ephrem, the harp of the Spirit (d. 373)

lines: A YOUNG MAN COMES HOME PROUD.
cards: This story isn't flattering to Basil, the same Basil from yesterday. He has come home from his studies, trained as a public speaker, and he's good at it, and he knows it.
Their younger brother Gregory, later bishop of Nyssa, wrote it down: Basil came back puffed up with his own eloquence, looking down on everyone. Waiting at home is his older sister.
She has no well-known teachers and no title. Her name is Macrina. And she set about turning him around.

teach.b: Macrina's story comes to us through her brother Gregory, in a short book called the Life of Macrina, so this is a portrait drawn by someone who loved her.

He says she was taught at home, not in the schools, and that the Psalms went with her through the whole day: when she got up, worked, rested, ate, and went to bed. That's where her learning came from.
When Basil came home proud, Gregory says, she drew him away from chasing a name for himself and toward a simple life given to God. Basil listened. Macrina didn't stop with her brother.
He says she persuaded their mother to live on the same level as the women who had served them, so the household became a community of prayer and work, sharing one table.
He says she also raised their youngest brother, Peter, almost as a mother would. Now the ending. Basil has died, and Gregory, heartbroken, travels to see his sister, and finds her dying too.
She lets him grieve for a little while. Then she starts to teach. They talk about death, the soul and the resurrection, and afterward Gregory writes the conversation down as a dialogue.
Look at how it's built. The well-known bishop asks the questions, and his sister gives the answers. Through most of it he doesn't use her name.
The Catholic Church honors Macrina as a saint, and her two pupils, Basil and Gregory, as saints too.

how: The Catholic Church honors Macrina as a saint, and Catholics who know her story often remember her alongside her brothers Basil and Gregory of Nyssa; Gregory's Life of Macrina is still read as spiritual reading.

o: an abbess who wrote the very first rule for nuns
the well-known teacher of public speaking in Athens
the sister who taught Basil and Gregory a life for God

p: came home proud of his speaking
the youngest, raised by his sister

s: Macrina learned her faith in the well-known schools
Gregory says she was taught at home, with the Psalms going with her through the day.
Gregory says Basil came home puffed up with his own eloquence
and his sister drew him toward a simple life given to God.
in the dialogue on the soul, Gregory teaches and Macrina asks
it's the other way round. he asks, she answers, and he calls her the Teacher.

games.q: you're Macrina, dying. your brother Gregory arrives heartbroken, still grieving Basil. what do you do?
o: send him away so he won't see you suffer.
let him grieve a little, then talk with him about death and the resurrection.
ask him to promise he'll write your life.
games.why: she lets him grieve for a while, then teaches. their conversation on the soul and the resurrection became his dialogue, with her as the Teacher.

practice: Bring to mind someone who taught you up close, not from a stage: an older sister, a grandmother, a coach, a teacher whose name you still remember.
Let one sentence of theirs come back in their voice, the way Gregory kept his sister's answers. If you pray, say their name to God, with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Macrina the teacher. The older sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, who taught them at home and at her deathbed, and whom her brother simply called the Teacher. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: teacher — what Gregory calls his sister in his dialogue on the soul.

carryVoice: Your line: the teacher of saints. Some of the best teachers never had a title. See you tomorrow.
